name: Database Indexing
intent: Keep a sorted lookup structure beside a table so queries can jump straight to the rows they need instead of reading every row.
scenario: A users table has hundreds of thousands of rows. The login page looks up one user by email, and every login scans the whole table.
problem: Without help, finding a row means reading the table from the start and checking each one (a full table scan). The cost grows with the size of the table, so a query that is instant on 1,000 rows takes seconds on 10 million, and every concurrent user adds to the load.

howItWorks.title: An index is a separate sorted structure
howItWorks.text: The database keeps, for a column, a sorted list of values with a pointer to each row. Because it is sorted, it can be searched by repeatedly halving the range (binary search), or walked as a tree (B-tree, the usual choice).

howItWorks.title: Lookups cost about log N instead of N
howItWorks.text: Finding one value among 500,000 takes around 19 comparisons instead of up to 500,000. Range queries find the start of the range and read forward, and prefix searches (LIKE 'Ma%') work the same way.

howItWorks.title: Not every query can use an index
howItWorks.text: An index helps when the query matches the sorted order: equality, ranges, prefixes, sorting. A search for a suffix or a substring (LIKE '%son'), or a function wrapped around the column, cannot use it and falls back to a full scan.

howItWorks.title: Indexes make writes slower
howItWorks.text: Every insert, update or delete must also update each index on the table, and indexes take disk space and memory. More indexes mean faster reads and slower writes.

howItWorks.title: Choose indexes from the queries you actually run
howItWorks.text: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY, put the most selective column (the one that narrows the rows down most) first in multi-column (composite) indexes, and use the database's query plan (EXPLAIN) to check that an index is really being used.

pros: Queries on indexed columns stay fast as tables grow
Makes sorting, range queries and joins much cheaper
Lets the database serve more users on the same hardware
cons: Every index slows inserts, updates and deletes
Wrong or unused indexes add cost for no benefit
Needs ongoing attention as query patterns change
whenToUse: Columns you filter, join or sort by frequently
Tables large enough that scans are noticeably slow
Columns with many distinct values (email, id), where an index narrows quickly
whenNotToUse: Small tables, where scanning is already fast
Columns with very few distinct values (a yes/no flag) where the index barely narrows anything
Write-heavy tables that are rarely queried
pitfalls: Indexing everything 'to be safe' and slowing every write
Writing queries that cannot use the index, such as LIKE '%text' or WHERE LOWER(email) = ...
Assuming an index is used without checking the query plan
Forgetting that a composite index only helps queries that use its leading columns

quiz.question: A table of 8 million orders is queried by user_id equality and takes about 2 seconds with no index. After adding a B-tree index on user_id the query takes a few milliseconds. Why is it so much faster?
options: The index keeps a copy of the table in memory, so the disk is never read.
The index lets the database scan the table in parallel on more cores.
The index removes duplicate user_id values, so there are fewer rows to read.
The sorted tree lets it jump to the matching rows in about log N steps.
quiz.explanation: A B-tree is sorted, so search halves the range at each step: roughly 23 steps for 8 million rows. It is not a cached copy or a parallel scan, and it does not delete rows.

quiz.question: A log table takes 30,000 inserts per second and has 12 indexes. It is rarely queried, and inserts have become slow. What is the best change?
options: Add one more composite index over all columns so lookups are fast, which also helps the planner.
Run ANALYZE more often so the planner picks better indexes and stale statistics stop slowing writes.
Drop the indexes that no regular query uses, since every insert must update each index.
Move the indexes to faster disks and keep all twelve.
quiz.explanation: Each index is maintained on every write, so unused ones are pure cost on a write-heavy table. A new index makes inserts slower still, and planner statistics do not change write cost.

quiz.question: A table has a composite index on (status, created_at), where status has only 3 values. The query WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50 still scans most of the table. What is the most accurate explanation and fix?
options: The index is fragmented after many updates, so rebuilding it will make the query use it.
The index is ordered by status first, so created_at alone cannot use it; index created_at first.
Status has few values, so a second index on status alone will let the database sort and filter.
Composite indexes cannot serve ORDER BY, so sorting must happen in the application.
quiz.explanation: The index is sorted by status first, so created_at alone is not in sorted order across the whole index. An index starting with created_at lets the database read the first 50 rows in order. Rebuilding does not change the column order.
